entities.name: Cleitus the Black
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Cleitus the Black (c. 374 BCE – 327 BCE) was a distinguished Macedonian cavalry commander and a close companion (hetairos) of Alexander the Great, whose life and death epitomize the complex loyalties and brutal power dynamics within Alexander's court during the conquest of the Achaemenid Persian Empire. His military prowess was instrumental in key victories, yet his ultimate significance stems from his dramatic murder by Alexander himself, an event that profoundly revealed the emperor's volatile temperament and the increasing strains within his inner circle as he adopted Eastern customs. Cleitus's fate served as a stark warning to other Macedonian nobles and highlighted the psychological toll of empire-building on its architects.

Cleitus served under Philip II and later became a trusted officer in Alexander's army, notably commanding the Royal Squadron of the Companion Cavalry. His defining moment of battlefield valor occurred at the Battle of the Granicus River in 334 BCE, where he famously saved Alexander's life by cutting off the arm of Spithridates, a Persian satrap, just as Spithridates was poised to strike Alexander from behind. He continued to lead the Companion Cavalry with distinction through campaigns in Asia Minor, Syria, and Egypt. In 328 BCE, during the campaign in Sogdiana, Cleitus was appointed satrap of Bactria and Sogdiana, a crucial administrative role in the newly conquered territories, though this appointment never fully materialized due to the events that followed.
